newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-March CPI may have more sting than balm.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-March CPI may have more sting than balm.

text.p: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) set for release on Tuesday could show that prices rose only moderately in March, but the report still could trouble the financial markets, analysts said.
"We're touting this CPI as a problematic number," said Elliott Platt, managing director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette.
Platt said he expects the March CPI to be up 0.3 percent and the core CPI, the index without its more volatile food and energy components, to be up 0.4 percent.

"Number one, hotel room rates have gone up a lot in the last couple of months and will find their way into the CPI," said Platt. "Number two, the excise tax on airline fares was reimposed in March. And three, apparel prices will be up."
Platt said he believes those three factors are mainly one-time events.
"Nonetheless, they can be a real market factor in the here and now," he said.
Kathy Bostjancic, money market analyst at UBS Securities, has a more subdued March CPI forecast of 0.2 percent rise, with a 0.3 percent core CPI gain.

"The CPI should continue to put in the benign performance we've been seeing in finished good prices in the first quarter of this year," said Bostjancic. "We're seeing some pickup in pipeline inflationary pressures, but not in the end use."
Bostjancic pointed to "some bubbling of inflation pressures in the Producer Price Index (PPI) as core crude and core intermediate prices began turning up."

On Friday, the Labor Department reported that March producer prices slipped 0.1 percent overall, but that the closely watched core PPI jumped 0.4 percent. At the intermediate stage of production, the core PPI was unchanged.
And at the earlier, crude production level, the core PPI index jumped 0.6 percent, the Labor Department said.
"Both the crude and intermediate core price trends turned from negative to positive year over year with Friday's PPI data so they're no longer deflationary," said Bostjancic.
"We know the Fed has openly declared war on strong demand numbers so the turning up of continued pipeline pressures would not be encouraging to the markets or the Fed," she said.
The Federal Open Market Commitee (FOMC) meets to consider interest rate policy again on May 20.

"We get two CPI readings, another Employment Cost Index and another payroll report between now and the next FOMC meeting," said Josh Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust.
With the economy showing no signs of a slowdown, the market is vulnerable to evidence of higher inflation, he said.

Another 25-basis-point interest-rate hike in May "is looking increasingly probable," said Feinman. "And if the economy doesn't show signs of slowing and you get an inflation scare, a 50-basis-point hike is not out of the question."
